items.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
items.one_liner: LLM planning failures stem more from predicate semantics than structural difficulty, proving that classical symbolic heuristics already estimate structural complexity well.
items.summary: Researchers examined seven STRIPS planning domains to distinguish structural difficulty from semantic vocabulary interpretation in LLM planning tasks. The zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic h_add outperformed learned alternatives like ridge regression, object count, and ARC for predicting structural difficulty on held-out domains with a mean Spearman |rho| of 0.931. To isolate semantic effects, the authors progressively renamed predicates while keeping states, transitions, and optimal plans identical, showing that valid LLM planning success dropped from 67.5% to 40.0% between 0% and 100% renaming. The findings indicate that symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty effectively, meaning future hybrid planning improvements should focus on modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than building new structural predictors.

LLM planning success drop: 67.5% to 40.0% between 0% and 100% predicate renaming
items.bottom_line: Improving LLM hybrid planning requires modeling how language models interpret predicate semantics rather than developing additional structural complexity predictors.

items.one_liner: A ClickFix campaign abuses the vintage Windows finger utility as a living-off-the-land binary to deploy infostealers and RMM tools.
items.summary: Threat actors are weaponizing a decades-old Windows utility, the finger command, in a novel ClickFix social engineering campaign targeting users searching for commercial services. Discovered by Huntress, the attack starts with sponsored search results for "amazon business" that redirect to a fake Amazon login page featuring a deceptive CAPTCHA. When users interact with the CAPTCHA, finger.exe is executed to fetch a remote .plan file, initiating a complex chain that installs IronPython, obfuscated loaders, Lumma Stealer, and a hidden NetSupport Client RMM tool. This living-off-the-land technique allows attackers to evade standard network detection mechanisms while delivering modular payloads.
key_facts: Malware: Lumma Stealer, NetSupport Client RMM
Initial Access: Google sponsored search results, fake CAPTCHA
items.bottom_line: Attackers are successfully abusing legacy built-in Windows utilities like finger to execute multi-stage malware chains via fake CAPTCHAs.

claims.text: The attack uses malicious Google search results related to Amazon and leverages the "finger" utility to launch a CAPTCHA that installs malware, including the Lumma stealer.
claims.support_span: The attack uses malicious Google search results related to Amazon and leverages the "finger" utility to launch a CAPTCHA that installs malware, including the Lumma stealer.

claims.text: A finger command kicks off a complex, multilayered attack chain that ends with the dropping of multiple payloads, including a pirated copy of the NetSupport Client remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool and a version of Lumma Stealer.

claims.text: Instead of moving directly from the user's action to one payload, a fake CAPTCHA used finger.exe, which executes a remote .plan file, installs IronPython, multiple obfuscated loaders, an alleged Lumma Stealer sample, and a hidden NetSupport Client.

items.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
items.one_liner: TURTLE is an unsupervised LLM agent framework that automatically generates evolving, difficult tool-use benchmarks.
items.summary: To improve AI assistant tool-use capabilities across applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack without relying on costly human supervision, researchers proposed TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution). TURTLE uses an Unsupervised Environment Design approach powered by proposer, solver, and feedback generator LLM agents to automatically evolve tasks for difficulty and diversity. Empirical evaluations across AppWorld, tau-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it showed that the framework successfully increased hard task generation by 165% on AppWorld while broadening task diversity and failure modes.
key_facts: Benchmark Improvement: 165% increase in hard tasks on AppWorld
items.bottom_line: Automated environment design frameworks like TURTLE can effectively scale the creation of complex, long-horizon tool-use benchmarks for AI assistants.
